outcome: I can explain scarcity, the factors of production and opportunity cost, and how different economic systems answer the basic economic questions.

learn.text:
Every society faces **[[scarcity]]**: human needs and wants are unlimited, but the resources to meet them are limited. Using resources faster than nature can renew them also threatens **[[sustainability]]**.

The resources are the **[[factors of production]]**:

- **[[Land]]**: natural resources, such as soil, water, fish and forests.
- **[[Labour]]**: human effort, physical and mental.
- **[[Capital]]**: man-made goods used to make other goods, such as tools, machines and boats.
- **[[Entrepreneurship]]**: organising the other factors and taking risks to start a business.

Scarcity forces **[[choice]]**. Every choice has an **[[opportunity cost]]**: the next best alternative given up. A **[[free good]]**, such as air, has no opportunity cost.

Every society must answer three **[[basic economic questions]]**: **what** (and how much) to produce, **how** to produce it, and **for whom**. A **[[free market economy]]** answers them through prices. A **[[planned economy]]** answers them through government decisions. A **[[mixed economy]]**, like most real economies, uses both.
learn.caption: Limited resources and unlimited wants create scarcity. Scarcity forces a choice, and every choice has an opportunity cost.

try.goal: Your class is shipwrecked on a quiet island. Build a village from what washes ashore, then run it three different ways.
try.intro:
**Level 1: What washed ashore?** Things wash up on the beach one at a time. Sort each into a factor of production, or call it a free good. Then the council must choose which projects to build first. Name the opportunity cost.

**Level 2: Three villages.** Answer what, how and for whom the way each economic system does. Each right answer builds part of the village.

**Level 3: System detective.** Read the clues about a village and name its economic system. Ask for another clue whenever you need one.

levels.title: What washed ashore?
levels.blurb: Sort 12 finds and name the opportunity cost. Get 10 right first time.

levels.title: Three villages
levels.blurb: Answer what, how and for whom in three systems. Get 8 of 9 right first time.

levels.title: System detective
levels.blurb: Name the system from clues. Solve 5 of 6 cases with your first guess.

items.name: Coconut palms
items.text: A grove of coconut palms grows behind the beach.
items.why: Trees that grow naturally are a **natural resource**, so they are land.

items.name: A freshwater spring
items.text: Clean water bubbles up from a spring in the rocks.
items.why: Water from nature is a natural resource: **land**. It is scarce here, because only one small spring must serve the whole village.

items.name: Fish in the lagoon
items.text: The lagoon is full of fish.
items.why: Fish in the wild are a **natural resource**, so they count as land.

items.name: Tomas, a strong swimmer
items.text: Tomas can dive for fish all day.
items.why: Tomas offers **human effort**. That is labour.

items.name: A trained nurse
items.text: Mei trained as a nurse for four years.
items.why: Mei's skill is **human effort** (mental and physical). Training makes her labour more productive, but it is still labour.

items.name: A fishing net
items.text: A strong fishing net washes up in one piece.
items.why: A net is **man-made** and is used to produce something else (fish). That is capital.

items.name: A hammer and a saw
items.text: A toolbox floats in with a hammer and a saw.
items.why: Tools are **man-made goods used to make other goods**: capital.

items.name: A canoe
items.text: A canoe drifts in. It can carry fish to the village.
items.why: The canoe is **man-made** and helps produce and transport fish. It is capital, not land.

items.name: Ana's bakery plan
items.text: Ana spots that everyone wants bread. She risks her savings to start a bakery and organises two helpers.
items.why: Ana **organises** the other factors and **takes a risk**. That is entrepreneurship.

items.name: Sam's ferry idea
items.text: Sam plans a ferry to the next island. He borrows a boat, hires a rower and hopes it pays off.
items.why: Sam **combines** land, labour and capital and **bears the risk** of failure: entrepreneurship.

items.name: Fresh sea air
items.text: There is plenty of fresh sea air for everyone.
items.why: Breathing it takes nothing away from anyone else, so there is **no opportunity cost**. It is a free good.

items.name: Sunshine on the beach
items.text: The sun shines on the whole beach.
items.why: Enjoying the sun uses up nothing that someone else wanted. **No opportunity cost**: a free good.

try.projectStory: The council has enough workers and tools for only **two** projects this season. Tap the four projects in order, from the one you want most to the one you want least.

costFeedback.right: Right. The opportunity cost is the **next best alternative** you gave up: your third choice. Your fourth choice was given up too, but it was not the next best.
costFeedback.both: Not quite. Opportunity cost is **only the next best** alternative given up, not every option you did not choose.
costFeedback.last: That was given up, but it was not the **next best**. Look at the project you ranked just below the ones you can afford.
costFeedback.none: Every choice gives something up. With scarce workers, choosing two projects means giving up the others.

villages.name: Market Village
villages.story: In Market Village, people own the land, tools and boats. Prices rise and fall with demand and supply. The council does almost nothing.
villages.strength: **Strength:** prices send signals, so firms make what people want, and competition pushes them to use resources efficiently.
villages.weakness: **Weakness:** people with little income may go without, and goods that cannot earn a profit (like streetlights) may not be made.

villages.name: Plan Village
villages.story: In Plan Village, the council owns the land, tools and boats. A planning committee makes every big decision.
villages.strength: **Strength:** the council can make sure everyone gets basic needs, such as food and health care.
villages.weakness: **Weakness:** without prices as signals, planners struggle to know what people want. Shortages of some goods and piles of others can follow.

villages.name: Harbour Village
villages.story: In Harbour Village, most shops and boats are private, but the council runs the clinic and the school, and collects taxes.
villages.strength: **Strength:** prices guide most choices, and the council steps in where the market fails or where incomes are very unequal.
villages.weakness: **Weakness:** people disagree about how much the council should do. Taxes can weaken incentives, and too little intervention can leave gaps.

what.market: Whatever buyers are willing and able to pay for, because firms follow prices and profit
what.planned: The planning committee decides, and sets a target for each good
what.mixed: Mostly what buyers pay for, but the council also provides some goods, such as schools and a clinic

how.market: Each firm chooses the cheapest method, to make the most profit
how.planned: The committee tells each workshop which methods and workers to use
how.mixed: Mostly firms choose, but council rules set limits, such as safety laws

forWhom.market: People who can pay the price, so it depends on their income
forWhom.planned: The committee shares goods out, for example by need or with ration coupons
forWhom.mixed: Mostly people who can pay, with taxes and benefits to help people on low incomes

try.villageWrong: That is how **{other}** answers this question. Think about who owns the resources in {village}, and who decides.

clues: Most shops and farms are owned by families and firms.
Every child goes to a free school paid for by taxes.
The government sets a minimum wage.
cases.explain: Private ownership and prices, plus government schools and a minimum wage: a **mixed economy**.

clues: A central office decides how many shoes each factory makes.
Prices are set by the state and rarely change.
Long queues form for bread, while unsold coats pile up.
cases.explain: The state decides output and prices. Shortages and surpluses are common because there are no price signals: a **planned economy**.

clues: Prices change every day with demand and supply.
There are no public schools or hospitals. Families pay for everything.
A firm that cannot make a profit closes down.
cases.explain: Prices and profit decide everything, and the government provides almost nothing: a **free market economy**.

clues: The railway is run by a state company.
Phone makers compete hard on price and features.
Families on low incomes receive cash benefits.
cases.explain: Competition between private firms, plus a state railway and benefits: a **mixed economy**.

clues: Land and factories belong to the state.
School leavers are told which job they will do.
Each farm must deliver a fixed amount of grain to the state.
cases.explain: The state owns the resources and directs workers and output: a **planned economy**.

clues: Roads are toll roads, built by private firms to earn a profit.
Doctors charge whatever patients are willing to pay.
The government only enforces contracts and protects property.
cases.explain: The government stays out of markets (laissez faire). Prices and profit answer every question: a **free market economy**.

check.prompt: A bakery uses an oven to bake bread. Which factor of production is the oven?

options.text: Capital
options.feedback: Yes. The oven is man-made and is used to produce another good (bread).

options.text: Land
options.feedback: Land is a natural resource. An oven is made by people.

options.text: Labour
options.feedback: Labour is human effort. The oven is a machine.

options.text: Entrepreneurship
options.feedback: Entrepreneurship is organising and risk-taking. The oven is a tool.

hints: Was the oven made by people, or does it come from nature?
Man-made goods used to make other goods are one factor of production.
check.worked: Example: a tractor on a farm is man-made and helps produce crops, so it is **capital**.
check.explanation: **Capital** is man-made goods used to produce other goods and services, such as machines, tools and buildings.

check.prompt: Which of these is the best example of **entrepreneurship**?

options.text: Lina uses her savings to open a café, hires two workers and rents a shop
options.feedback: Yes. Lina organises land, labour and capital and takes the risk that the café fails.

options.text: Lina works long shifts as a waiter in a café
options.feedback: That is labour: human effort for a wage.

options.text: Lina buys a new coffee machine for the café
options.feedback: The coffee machine is capital. Entrepreneurship is the organising and risk-taking.

options.text: Lina owns the land the café is built on
options.feedback: Land is a natural resource. Owning it is not the same as organising a business.

hints: Look for organising other factors and taking a risk.
Who could lose money if the business fails?
check.worked: Example: Ravi borrows money to start a bike repair shop and hires a mechanic. He organises the factors and bears the risk: **entrepreneurship**.
check.explanation: **Entrepreneurship** means organising the other factors of production and taking risks to start or run a business.

check.prompt: Why is air usually called a **free good**?

options.text: Using it has no opportunity cost, because there is enough for everyone
options.feedback: Yes. Breathing air does not take it away from anyone else.

options.text: Nobody has to pay a price for it in a shop
options.feedback: Many things have no price but still have an opportunity cost. A free good has no opportunity cost at all.

options.text: The government provides it
options.feedback: Goods the government provides still use scarce resources, so they are not free goods.

options.text: It is a natural resource
options.feedback: Many natural resources, like oil, are scarce. Being natural does not make a good free.

hints: Does your breathing stop anyone else from breathing?
check.worked: Example: sunshine on a large beach. One person enjoying it does not reduce what others get, so there is no opportunity cost.
check.explanation: A **free good** is not scarce, so using it has **no opportunity cost**. A good with a zero price can still be scarce.

check.prompt: This chart shows why economics exists. Choose the label for each letter.

diagram.title: The problem of choice
diagram.description: Two boxes on the left, one for wants and one for resources, both point to a box in the middle. Arrows lead from it to a second box and then a third box on the right. Each box has a letter.

slots.feedback: A sits next to unlimited wants. It is the other half of the problem: limited resources.
Unlimited wants and limited resources together create scarcity.
Every choice gives up the next best alternative: the opportunity cost.

hints: Start with A: it pairs with unlimited wants.
The order is: the problem, what it forces us to do, and the cost of doing it.
check.worked: Example: a town has one field (limited) and many people who want a park, a car park and houses (unlimited wants). That is scarcity. The council must choose. If it builds houses, the park it gives up is the opportunity cost.
check.explanation: Unlimited wants and **limited resources** create **scarcity**. Scarcity forces **choice**, and every choice has an **opportunity cost**.

check.prompt: Jo can work at a shop for $90, babysit for $70, or go to the beach. She chooses to study instead. What is the opportunity cost of studying?

options.text: The $90 from working at the shop
options.feedback: Yes, if the shop job is her next best alternative. Opportunity cost is only the next best option given up.

options.text: $160: the shop pay plus the babysitting pay
options.feedback: She could only do one of these, so only the next best alternative counts.

options.text: Nothing, because studying is free
options.feedback: Studying uses her time. The cost is what she could have done with that time.

options.text: The beach
options.feedback: Only if the beach was her next best choice. Here the question suggests the shop job is worth most to her.

hints: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up.
Can she do the shop job and babysit in the same hours?
check.worked: Example: Sam chooses to play football instead of earning $50 at a café or $30 mowing lawns. If the café job is his next best choice, the opportunity cost is $50 of café pay.
check.explanation: **Opportunity cost** is the value of the **next best** alternative given up. Jo can only do one thing with that time, so it is not the sum of all options.

check.prompt: In a **planned economy**, how is the question **what to produce** answered?

options.text: The government decides and sets output targets
options.feedback: Yes. Planners choose what is made and how much.

options.text: Firms make whatever earns the most profit
options.feedback: That is how a free market economy answers it.

options.text: Consumers vote on every product
options.feedback: Planned economies do not run on votes for each product. The state decides.

options.text: Prices rise until the right amount is made
options.feedback: Prices guide output in a market economy. In a planned economy the state usually sets prices.

hints: Who owns the resources in a planned economy?
Think about who makes decisions instead of prices.
check.worked: Example: a planning office decides the country will make 2 million pairs of shoes and 10,000 tractors this year, and tells factories their targets.
check.explanation: In a **planned economy**, the government owns most resources and decides **what, how and for whom** to produce.

check.prompt: A country has private firms competing for customers, but the government runs the hospitals and taxes high incomes more heavily. What kind of economy is it?

options.text: A mixed economy
options.feedback: Yes. Markets answer most questions, and the government steps in for health care and fairness.

options.text: A free market economy
options.feedback: A pure free market economy would leave hospitals to private firms and avoid redistributing income.

options.text: A planned economy
options.feedback: Private firms competing for customers shows prices are doing most of the work.

options.text: There is not enough information
options.feedback: There is: both private markets and government provision are described.

hints: Are prices doing some of the work?
Is the government also doing some of the work?
check.worked: Example: shops and restaurants are private, but schools and roads are paid for by taxes. Both markets and government answer the basic questions: a mixed economy.
check.explanation: A **mixed economy** uses markets for most goods and government intervention for some goods and to reduce inequality. Almost every real economy is mixed.

check.prompt: Which statement best describes a **weakness** of a free market economy?

options.text: People with low incomes may not afford basic goods, and some useful goods may not be provided
options.feedback: Yes. In a free market, goods go to those who can pay, and goods that cannot earn a profit may be missing.

options.text: There are no price signals, so firms cannot tell what people want
options.feedback: That is a weakness of a planned economy. Free markets are full of price signals.

options.text: The government makes too many decisions
options.feedback: In a free market economy the government makes very few decisions.

options.text: Firms have no incentive to be efficient
options.feedback: Competition and profit give firms a strong incentive to be efficient.

hints: In a free market, how is the question 'for whom' answered?
Think about people with little income, and goods nobody can charge for.
check.worked: Example: in a free market, private firms might not build a streetlight, because they cannot make people pay to use the light.
check.explanation: Free markets can be efficient, but they may leave **inequality** and fail to provide some goods. This is one reason most economies are mixed.

check.prompt: Fishers catch fish faster than the fish can breed, so each year there are fewer fish. Which idea does this show best?

options.text: Scarcity and a threat to sustainability
options.feedback: Yes. Using a resource faster than it can renew means future generations have less.

options.text: Fish are a free good
options.feedback: Fish are scarce: catching one leaves fewer for others.

options.text: The fish are capital
options.feedback: Wild fish are a natural resource, so they are land.

options.text: A planned economy
options.feedback: The question is about using a resource up, not about who makes decisions.

hints: Is the resource getting scarcer over time?
check.worked: Example: cutting down a forest faster than trees grow back. Wood becomes scarcer and the forest may never recover: a sustainability problem.
check.explanation: Resources are **scarce**. Using them faster than they renew is **unsustainable**, because it reduces what future generations can use.

explain.prompt: Choose one village. Explain how its economic system answers the three basic economic questions. Give one strength and one weakness.
frames: In ___, the question of what to produce is answered by ___.
How to produce is decided by ___, because ___.
One strength of this system is ___.
checklist: I answered all three questions: what, how and for whom.
I said who owns resources and who makes decisions.
I gave one strength and one weakness, with a reason for each.

teacherNotes: Level 1 is a good opener for 1.1: project the beach and let the class vote on each find before a student taps. The canoe and the nurse cause the best debates (capital vs land; labour with training). In the opportunity cost task, students rank four projects; the answer depends on their own ranking, so ask two students with different rankings to compare. Level 2 builds the village one answer at a time, then shows a strength and a weakness of each system: use these for an evaluation discussion. Level 3 is a detective game; students can ask for more clues. Discussion idea: is any real economy a pure free market or a pure planned economy?
